title: Odile and the Visitor
premise: Folklorist Beatrix Reyes arrives in the isolated village of Sainte-Odile to record a lullaby that no one will sing twice, staying in the late Odile Marchand's house at the village's edge. She discovers that every photograph taken inside the house now shows an extra chair, and that the chair moves closer each night; the song is not a lullaby but an invitation, and by recording it she has answered it. As the villagers who once welcomed her turn away and the Visitor takes the shapes of people she has lost, Beatrix learns the house survives only by feeding it a keeper, and that Odile's 'found family' of previous folklorists all chose to stay. In the end, Beatrix burns her recordings and sings the song backward at dawn, breaking the invitation but binding herself to the house as its new guardian—alive, but no longer able to leave.
about_author: Quentin Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in rural France before turning to fiction. They write horror about the things we invite in without meaning to, and live near the sea with too many unlabelled cassette tapes.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Beatrix Reyes, POV. Arriving in Sainte-Odile to document a lullaby collected once in 1911 and never again, she finds the villagers warm but evasive, ending every conversation when the song comes up. Old Marcel hums four bars, then goes pale and stops. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease as Beatrix realizes the silence itself is a kind of testimony.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. She takes lodging in Odile Marchand's empty house on the hill—the only place available—and finds it oddly prepared: fresh linens, a stocked pantry, a journal half-filled in Odile's hand. The last entry reads only: 'It likes the new ones best.' Emotional beat: comfort curdling into the sense of being expected rather than welcomed.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Reviewing her field photographs, she notices a wooden chair in every shot of the kitchen—a chair that wasn't there. Comparing images night by night, she finds it inching closer to the table where she eats alone. Emotional beat: rational denial cracking; documentation, her form of prayer, becomes evidence of haunting.

chapters.title: What the Village Won't Say
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, intercut with Marcel's 1974 diary excerpts. She presses the villagers for answers and meets locked doors; the priest gives her salt and says nothing else. The diary reveals Odile wasn't the first keeper—there have been six, each a visiting scholar who stayed. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as hospitality flips to quiet expulsion.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Desperate for the full song, she plays her partial recording of Marcel's four bars in the house. The tape continues past where he stopped—someone else's voice, older, singing verses in a dialect no one speaks anymore. The chair is now at the table. Emotional beat: dread and a terrible scholarly thrill; she has invited something in with her own equipment.

chapters.title: Visitors
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. The Visitor begins wearing faces: her dead mother at the window, her estranged brother on the stairs, each gently urging her to sit, to rest, to stay. She nearly does. A scratch on her arm won't heal, and the house feels warmer each hour. Emotional beat: grief weaponized; the horror of being loved by something hungry.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, reading Odile's hidden letters. She learns the truth: the house stands on a threshold, and the thing beyond it keeps the village safe from something worse—for a price. Each keeper was 'invited' through the song, then bound. Odile's final letter begs whoever finds it to run before sunrise. Emotional beat: the corrupt bargain revealed; power as protection and prison both.

chapters.title: The Village Remembers
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Marcel, alternating POV. On the sixth night the whole village gathers below the hill—not to help her, but to watch, as they watched the others. Marcel, guilt-ridden, slips her the missing verse he's carried since childhood. Emotional beat: betrayal and unexpected grace; found family forming in the worst possible place.

chapters.title: Sunrise Negotiation
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Trapped inside as the doors seal and the Visitor offers her everything—her mother back, her brother forgiven—if she'll only take the chair. She burns the recordings, sings the song backward with Marcel's verse, and the house screams. Dawn breaks with her alive at the table, the chair empty, the door open. Emotional beat: climax; defiance priced in blood.

chapters.title: Keeper
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, epilogue months later. The village welcomes her now, brings bread, calls her by name—but the roads out of Sainte-Odile feel wrong whenever she walks them, and the chair waits by the table, patient, companionable. She writes to a young folklorist: don't come. Then adds directions anyway. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; survival as a sentence, family as a cage she chooses.
